name: Straight razor

card.summary: The traditional folding open razor; popular again as a ritual and a craft, but no studies test its effect on skin or appearance.
card.note: Requires stropping and honing; cuts are a recognised risk for beginners.

quick.overview:
A straight razor is a single steel blade that folds into a handle. It was the standard shaving tool before safety and electric razors and has seen renewed interest since around 2008.

It is a grooming tool whose effects last until hair regrows. No clinical studies compare it with other razors.
quick.mechanism: A very sharp edge, kept aligned by stropping and sharpened by honing, slices hair at the skin surface when drawn at a shallow angle.
quick.risks: Nicks and cuts are the main hazards, especially for beginners. Carbon steel blades rust without care, and some blade styles are fragile or bite.

lead: A straight razor, also called a cut-throat or open razor, is a single-bladed razor whose blade folds into a protective handle, known as the scales. Men use it for traditional wet shaving to get a clean-shaven face, sharp beard lines and a neat jaw and neck, and many choose it for the closeness and the grooming ritual.[1][2][3]

Blades are made of high-carbon or stainless steel and are kept sharp by the owner or a professional through honing and stropping.[1] Wet shaving in general involves softening the hair with warm water or a hot towel, applying lather with a brush, and often shaving in several passes.[3] Barbers have offered straight-razor shaves for generations, and one T Nation member calls a barber's straight-razor shave great.[5]

Demand fell through the 20th century as safety razors and then electric razors spread, but has grown again since about 2008, with commentators citing nostalgia, long-term cost, reduced waste and craftsmanship.[1] Dermatology sources note that very close shaving can lead to razor bumps in people with curly beard hair, and suggest techniques such as shaving with the grain and leaving a small amount of stubble.[4]

chain: Sharp single blade cuts hair at skin level
A close, even shave with crisp beard and neck lines
A clean, groomed face and jawline
angle.text: The blade removes facial hair at skin level, and users value it for crisp edges along the beard line, cheeks and neck. The look is a clean-shaven face that shows the jaw.

infobox: Metal razors in ancient Egypt; Sheffield production from about 1680[1]

paras: Blades are classified by point shape (round, French, square, spike, Spanish or barber's notch), by grind from flat wedge to full or extra hollow, and by width.[1] More hollow grinds make the blade flexible and the edge delicate, so it shaves closer but needs more skill and suits lighter beards.[1] Scales are made of acrylic, celluloid, bone, horn or wood.[1] Carbon steel is easier to hone but rusts if neglected, while stainless steel resists rust but is harder to hone.[1] Grokipedia notes that a shallow blade angle of about 30 degrees is typically used.[2]

Bronze razors appear in Egypt during the New Kingdom, and gold and copper razors have been found in tombs from the fourth millennium BC.[1] Sheffield manufacturers listed narrow-bladed folding steel razors in 1680, and Benjamin Huntsman's cast-steel process around 1740 enabled hollow-ground blades.[1] A guarded razor was designed by Jean-Jacques Perret in 1762.[2]

Gillette's disposable-blade safety razor arrived in the late 19th and early 20th century, and electric razors further reduced the straight razor's share from the 1950s.[1] Barber shaving revenue fell from roughly half of income around 1898 to about a tenth by 1939, by one New York barber's estimate.[3] Interest returned from about 2008; the 2012 film Skyfall is credited with boosting sales, and the German maker Dovo reportedly went from fewer than 8,000 units a year in 2006 to about 3,000 a month.[1]

Wet-shaving guidance describes warming the skin with water or a hot towel, applying a lather or lubricant, shaving with the grain and using minimal pressure; irritation is linked to blunt blades, dry shaving, pressure and shaving against the grain.[3] Aftershave may be used to reduce irritation.[3]

Pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps) occurs when closely cut hair regrows into the skin, and is most common with curly or coarse beard hair.[4] Dermatology guidance includes shaving with the grain, using a sharp single-blade razor, softening the beard first and not shaving too close, with a stubble length of about 0.5 to 1 mm suggested in studies.[4]

Inexperienced users may nick or pinch the skin, and round or muted points are recommended for beginners, according to Wikipedia.[1] Very thin extra-hollow blades are fragile, and Spanish points can bite during shaving or stropping.[1] Celluloid scales can combust spontaneously at high temperature.[1] Wet shaving generally is described as making cuts more likely than other methods.[3] In a forum thread about trimming body hair, one member advises against using a straight razor.[6]

Straight razors appear in grooming discussion mainly as a barbershop service or a personal ritual. Gear is typically paired with a brush, lather and strop.[1][3] A T Nation member in a transformation challenge thread suggests shaving with a straight razor for a clean look.[7]
No studies found of straight-razor shaving for appearance outcomes. Dermatology literature on shaving is summarised in references on pseudofolliculitis barbae.[4]

timeline.event: Sheffield makers list narrow-bladed folding steel razors.[1]
Huntsman's cast-steel process adopted for hollow-ground blades.[1]
